_note: Pharmacology flashcards. Keys are 'pharmacology__<Section>__<Subsection>'. Card shape: {id, front, back}. Seed examples included; replace/extend freely.

subsections: Drugs Used in CKD / Renal Replacement
Drugs Commonly Implicated in Specific Conditions

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what is the mechanism of action on the renin-angiotensin system?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Block angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) -> less angiotensin II -> arteriolar vasodilation plus less aldosterone (so Na+ and water loss) -> lower BP and reduced cardiac afterload.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: why do they cause dry cough and angioedema?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They also slow bradykinin breakdown. The accumulating bradykinin is what causes the dry cough and angioedema.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what is their place in hypertension therapy?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: First-line if under 55 and not of Black African/Caribbean origin; first-line at any age in type 2 diabetes (renoprotective). In Black African/Caribbean patients needing an A-drug, prefer an ARB instead.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what are the main indications besides hypertension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (improves survival - start early, titrate to max tolerated dose); post-MI secondary prevention, especially with LV dysfunction; and diabetic nephropathy / proteinuric CKD (lowers intraglomerular pressure, slows progression).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: why are they renoprotective in diabetic nephropathy / proteinuric CKD?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They lower intraglomerular pressure, which slows progression of the kidney disease.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: why are they contraindicated in pregnancy, and what is the alternative?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Teratogenic - cause fetal renal damage and oligohydramnios. Switch to labetalol or nifedipine if planning pregnancy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: why are they contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: These kidneys depend on angiotensin II to hold up the GFR, so an ACEi precipitates acute kidney injury.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what absolute contraindication applies to a patient with prior ACEi angioedema?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Never re-challenge - do not restart an ACE inhibitor.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what situations warrant caution (not absolute contraindication)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Severe aortic stenosis (risk of hypotension), volume depletion / high-dose diuretics (start low, dose at night), and a baseline K+ >5.0.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what are the typical once-daily dose ranges for ramipril, lisinopril and perindopril?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Ramipril 1.25-10 mg OD; lisinopril 5-40 mg OD; perindopril 4-8 mg OD.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: how common is the dry cough and what do you do about it?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Occurs in ~15% (bradykinin-mediated). If intolerable, switch to an ARB - same benefits, no bradykinin, so the cough settles.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: how do you manage first-dose hypotension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Give the first dose at bedtime, start low, and warn the patient. It is worse if the patient is already on a diuretic.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: at what K+ level do you act on hyperkalaemia, and how?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: If K+ >5.5, reduce or stop the ACEi and review other potassium-raising drugs.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: how do you interpret a rising creatinine after starting?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: A rise of <=30% (with K+ <=5.5) is expected and fine - do not stop. A bigger jump suggests renal artery stenosis - stop and investigate.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: how do you manage angioedema?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Stop immediately and treat as an emergency (airway risk; commoner in Black patients). Never restart.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: which minor side effects (besides cough) should you know?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Taste disturbance and a mild rise in urea.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: why do NSAIDs cause AKI when combined, and what is the 'triple whammy'?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole while the ACEi dilates the efferent one -> filtration pressure collapses -> AKI. The triple whammy is ACEi + NSAID + diuretic. Avoid, or monitor U&Es and keep hydrated.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: which drugs cause additive hyperkalaemia, and what is the rule?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: ARBs, spironolactone/eplerenone, amiloride, trimethoprim and K+ supplements. Don't routinely combine ACEi + ARB, and check K+ after adding an aldosterone antagonist.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what is the interaction with lithium?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Reduced renal excretion of lithium -> lithium toxicity -> monitor levels.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: how do you avoid first-dose hypotension when a patient is on a diuretic?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Omit the diuretic dose beforehand or dose the ACEi at night.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what U&E monitoring schedule is required?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check U&Es before starting, again at 1-2 weeks, and after every dose increase - to catch a big creatinine rise (unmasks renal artery stenosis) and hyperkalaemia early.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what is the 'sick-day rule'?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Recheck and hold the ACEi during any dehydrating illness (vomiting, diarrhoea, sepsis).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what does captopril's structure mean for its use?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Short-acting (BD/TDS) with a thiol group -> more taste disturbance and rash. Now mainly used for neonatal or test dosing.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: which agents are the long-acting once-daily prodrugs used in practice?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Ramipril, perindopril and trandolapril - long-acting prodrugs given once daily.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what is special about lisinopril's pharmacology?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is not a prodrug (already active) and is renally cleared, so it accumulates in renal impairment - use lower doses.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ACE inhibitors: what is the active metabolite of enalapril and its IV form?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Enalapril is a prodrug hydrolysed to enalaprilat (the active metabolite); enalaprilat itself is the intravenous form.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs (losartan, candesartan, valsartan, irbesartan): What is the mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Block the angiotensin II type-1 (AT1) receptor -> vasodilation and less aldosterone (same downstream effect as an ACEi), but without raising bradykinin -> so no dry cough.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: Why do they not cause the dry cough seen with ACE inhibitors?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They act at the AT1 receptor without raising bradykinin. It is the accumulation of bradykinin (from ACEi) that causes the cough, so ARBs avoid it.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What is their first-line niche in hypertension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Same as an ACEi -> patients under 55 or with type 2 diabetes. They are the go-to when an ACEi has caused cough.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs vs ACEi: Which is preferred in Black African/Caribbean patients needing an A-drug?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: An ARB is preferred over an ACEi (NICE), including in those with type 2 diabetes.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What are the main indications besides hypertension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heart failure with reduced EF (alternative to ACEi) and diabetic nephropathy / proteinuric CKD (renoprotective).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What are the absolute contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Pregnancy (teratogenic, same as ACEi) and bilateral renal artery stenosis (precipitates AKI).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: In what situations should they be used with caution?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Volume depletion, baseline K+ >5.0, and severe aortic stenosis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What are the typical starting (and maximum) doses of losartan, candesartan, and valsartan?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Losartan 50 mg OD (up to 100 mg); candesartan 8 mg OD (up to 32 mg); valsartan 80-160 mg OD.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: How do you act on hyperkalaemia caused by them?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check K+; reduce or stop the ARB if K+ >5.5.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: How much rise in creatinine after starting is acceptable, and what does a bigger jump suggest?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: A rise of up to 30% is acceptable (same rule as ACEi); a bigger jump -> suspect renal artery stenosis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What are the notable side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hyperkalaemia, rising creatinine, and first-dose hypotension with dizziness. No cough (key advantage over ACEi) and angioedema is rare.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What is the interaction with NSAIDs?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive AKI risk (the triple whammy when combined with a diuretic) -> avoid or monitor U&Es.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: Which drugs raise the risk of hyperkalaemia when combined, and what combination must be avoided?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: K+-raising drugs (spironolactone, trimethoprim, K+ supplements) -> hyperkalaemia. Never combine an ARB with an ACEi.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What is the interaction with lithium?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Reduced lithium excretion -> toxicity -> monitor lithium levels.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: When should U&Es be checked?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Before starting, at 1-2 weeks, and after each dose increase -> to catch a big creatinine rise (renal artery stenosis) or hyperkalaemia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What is the sick-day rule?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hold the ARB during dehydrating illness.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What is special about losartan among the class?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is mildly uricosuric (a small bonus in gout). It is a short-acting parent converted (via CYP2C9/3A4) to the active metabolite EXP3174 (E-3174), which is more potent and longer-acting and gives most of the 24-hour effect.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What is notable about candesartan individually?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is long-acting and also has migraine-prophylaxis evidence.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: Which agents have strong renoprotection data?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Irbesartan and valsartan.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: What is the key high-yield pearl summarising their role?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They are the ACEi alternative when cough is the problem -> same benefits, no bradykinin. They share the same pregnancy and hyperkalaemia cautions, and an ACEi + ARB must never be combined.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Calcium channel blockers (dihydropyridines): what is the mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block L-type Ca2+ channels in vascular smooth muscle -> arteriolar vasodilation -> lower BP.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Calcium channel blockers (dihydropyridines): why are they described as vascular-selective?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They act selectively on vascular smooth muscle with little effect on heart rate or contractility (unlike rate-limiting CCBs).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine): where do they sit in the NICE stepwise treatment of hypertension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: First-line (step 1) if aged >=55, or Black African/Caribbean at any age - in either case without type 2 diabetes.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Dihydropyridine CCBs: how do they help in angina?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They reduce afterload and cause coronary vasodilation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Nimodipine: what is its specific indication?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: To prevent cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) - it is CNS-selective and not used for hypertension.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Dihydropyridine CCBs: why give with caution in severe aortic stenosis?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Vasodilation can precipitate collapse. Also use caution in unstable angina and marked ankle oedema.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Dihydropyridine CCBs: which CCB is safest in stable heart failure, and what should be avoided?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Amlodipine is the safest CCB in stable heart failure; avoid CCBs in cardiogenic shock.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Amlodipine: what is the typical oral dose for hypertension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 5 mg once daily, up to 10 mg.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Nimodipine: what is the dose for subarachnoid haemorrhage prophylaxis?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 60 mg every 4 hours.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Dihydropyridine CCBs: what is the most characteristic side effect and why does it occur?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Ankle/peripheral oedema - very common and dose-related, caused by precapillary (arteriolar) dilation, not fluid overload.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Dihydropyridine CCBs: how do you manage the ankle oedema they cause?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Diuretics don't help (it isn't fluid overload); instead reduce the dose or add an ACE inhibitor/ARB.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Dihydropyridine CCBs: which vasodilation-related side effects occur besides oedema?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Flushing, headache, and palpitations (reflex tachycardia); also gum hypertrophy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Dihydropyridine CCBs: why avoid grapefruit juice, and which drug is especially affected?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 -> higher drug levels and hypotension, especially with felodipine.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Amlodipine: what is the key interaction with simvastatin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Amlodipine raises simvastatin levels -> cap simvastatin at 20 mg.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Dihydropyridine CCBs: what should be monitored?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Blood pressure for response, and ankle oedema (dose-related arteriolar dilation, not fluid overload, so it doesn't respond to diuretics).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Amlodipine: what pharmacokinetic feature allows once-daily dosing?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It has a long half-life, so it is given once daily; it is also safe in stable heart failure.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Nicardipine: what is its notable formulation/use?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Available IV for hypertensive emergencies.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil/diltiazem): what is the mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Block L-type Ca2+ channels in both blood vessels AND the heart -> vasodilation plus negative chronotropy (slows the SA/AV node) and negative inotropy (reduces contractility).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Non-dihydropyridine CCBs: how do they differ from dihydropyridines in where they act?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They act on the heart as well as vessels, producing negative chronotropy and negative inotropy in addition to vasodilation (not vessel-selective).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: what are the main clinical uses?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Rate control in AF/SVT; angina (including when a beta-blocker is contraindicated); and, less commonly, hypertension.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: which non-dihydropyridine feature makes them useful for angina when beta-blockers can't be used?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Their negative chronotropy/inotropy reduces cardiac workload, so they can substitute for a beta-blocker in angina when one is contraindicated.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: why must they NEVER be combined with a beta-blocker?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive AV-node block -> severe bradycardia, complete heart block, and asystole.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: what cardiac conduction/rhythm states are contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 2nd-3rd degree AV block, significant bradycardia, and VT or WPW with AF.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: why are they contraindicated in heart failure with reduced EF?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Their negative inotropy reduces contractility further -> cardiac decompensation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil: what is the typical dosing?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 40-120 mg TDS (or a modified-release preparation once daily).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Diltiazem: what is the typical dosing?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Modified-release 90-360 mg once daily (OD).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: what are the key cardiac side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bradycardia and AV block, due to negative chronotropy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil: which very common non-cardiac side effect is characteristic?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Constipation (very common with verapamil).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: what side effects arise from negative inotropy and vasodilation?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Worsening heart failure (negative inotropy) and ankle oedema.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: why is combining them with a beta-blocker a dangerous interaction?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It causes additive AV-node block -> bradycardia/asystole; the combination should be avoided.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil: what is its interaction with digoxin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Verapamil raises digoxin levels -> risk of digoxin toxicity.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: what is the interaction with simvastatin and its mechanism?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They raise simvastatin levels via CYP3A4 inhibition.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: what is the MHRA dose limit for co-prescribed simvastatin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Simvastatin maximum 20 mg/day, because of CYP3A4 inhibition raising statin levels.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: what monitoring is needed, especially with digoxin or a beta-blocker?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Monitor HR, BP and ECG (AV conduction), particularly when co-prescribed with digoxin or a beta-blocker.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil vs diltiazem: how do they compare in negative inotropy and tolerability?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Verapamil is the most negatively inotropic and causes the most constipation (avoid in heart failure); diltiazem is intermediate (rate control plus vasodilation) and better tolerated.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil/diltiazem: what is the single most important prescribing pearl?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Never give with a beta-blocker due to the risk of AV-node standstill.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Verapamil: which two problems does the exam pearl specifically link to it?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Constipation and worsening of heart failure.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (bisoprolol/metoprolol): what is the mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Block β1-adrenoceptors (mainly cardiac) -> reduce heart rate, contractility and AV conduction -> lower cardiac output and BP. They also reduce renin release.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: what does 'cardioselective' mean and what is its limitation?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Relatively β1 > β2 selective (e.g. bisoprolol, metoprolol). Selectivity is lost at higher doses.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: which agents improve survival in heart failure with reduced EF, and how are they started?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bisoprolol, carvedilol and nebivolol improve survival. Start low, go slow, and only when the patient is stable.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: list the main indications.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heart failure (reduced EF), angina and post-MI secondary prevention, AF rate control and arrhythmias, and hypertension (as a step-4 add-on).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: where do they sit in hypertension treatment?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Step-4 add-on -> not first-line unless there is another indication.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: why are they cautioned/relatively contraindicated in asthma?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: β2 blockade -> bronchospasm. Relative CI; use a cardioselective agent with caution only if unavoidable.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: list the cardiac contraindications.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Severe bradycardia, 2nd-3rd degree heart block, decompensated heart failure, and cardiogenic shock.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: which drug class must never be co-prescribed, and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Never with verapamil/diltiazem -> risk of severe bradycardia / AV block; avoid.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Bisoprolol: what is the dosing in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Start 1.25-2.5 mg once daily and titrate up to 10 mg. Start low.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Bisoprolol: what is the maximum dose in hypertension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 20 mg once daily (start low).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: list the common side effects.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bradycardia, fatigue/lethargy, cold peripheries, bronchospasm (β2), erectile dysfunction, and vivid dreams (with lipophilic agents).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: what important effect do they have in diabetics?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They mask the tachycardia of hypoglycaemia -> loss of an early hypo warning sign.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: what are the key drug interactions?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Verapamil/diltiazem -> severe bradycardia/AV block (avoid); insulin/sulfonylureas -> masks hypo warning signs; NSAIDs -> blunt the antihypertensive effect.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: what monitoring is needed when uptitrating in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Monitor HR and BP, uptitrate slowly, and expect transient early worsening.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: why must they never be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Abrupt withdrawal -> rebound tachycardia / angina / MI. Taper down instead.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Bisoprolol: what are its distinguishing features?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Highly β1-selective and once daily -> first choice in heart failure/hypertension.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Metoprolol: what are its distinguishing features?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: β1-selective; also used IV for acute rate control.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Nebivolol: what makes it unique among beta-blockers?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: The most β1-selective agent; uniquely causes nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilation (via β3/eNOS) -> vasodilating and metabolically favourable, used in elderly HF/HTN.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): what is carvedilol's mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Non-selective beta-blocker (blocks beta1 and beta2) plus alpha1-blockade. The alpha1 effect adds vasodilation, which reduces afterload and is useful in heart failure.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): what distinguishes carvedilol from a simple beta-blocker?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It adds alpha1-blockade (causing vasodilation) on top of non-selective beta-blockade, making it prognostic in heart failure. It is given twice daily.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): what are the indications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (one of the three prognostic beta-blockers with bisoprolol and nebivolol), plus hypertension and angina.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: which three beta-blockers are prognostic in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Carvedilol, bisoprolol, and nebivolol.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): what are the contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Asthma (non-selective -> higher bronchospasm risk), decompensated heart failure, and severe bradycardia / heart block.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): why is it contraindicated in asthma?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is non-selective (blocks beta2), giving a higher bronchospasm risk than cardioselective agents.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): what is the dosing in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Start 3.125 mg BD and titrate slowly up to 25 mg BD.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): what side effect is added by its alpha1-blockade?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Postural hypotension / dizziness (from alpha1 block), especially with the first dose.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): how does its bronchospasm risk compare to cardioselective agents?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bronchospasm risk is higher than with cardioselective beta-blockers, because carvedilol is non-selective.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): which drugs must never be co-prescribed, and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Never with verapamil or diltiazem -> additive AV block -> bradycardia, heart block, or asystole.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): why should it not be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia, angina, and hypertension. Taper the dose instead.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): what is the interaction with insulin/sulfonylureas?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It may mask the warning signs of hypoglycaemia (except sweating).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): what should be monitored?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heart rate and blood pressure, aiming for a resting HR that is not persistently below 50-55.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): what monitoring is specific to heart failure use?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Uptitrate slowly and watch for transient worsening of heart failure and fluid retention.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (carvedilol): what is the high-yield exam pearl?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It adds alpha1 vasodilation to beta-blockade, making it good in heart failure, but being non-selective it is worse in asthma and causes a postural drop.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): what is atenolol's receptor selectivity and solubility?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Atenolol is beta1-selective and water-soluble (hydrophilic).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): what are the consequences of atenolol being water-soluble (hydrophilic)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Being hydrophilic, it is renally excreted and crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly -> fewer CNS effects, but it accumulates in renal impairment.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): what are the main indications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Angina, arrhythmias, and post-MI. Historically used for hypertension too.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): why is it now less favoured for hypertension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It has weaker stroke-prevention evidence than other agents, so it is no longer first-line for HTN outcomes.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): what are the contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Asthma, severe bradycardia / 2nd-3rd degree heart block, and decompensated heart failure.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): what is the typical dose?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Atenolol 25-100 mg once daily (OD).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): why does it cause fewer CNS side effects than other beta-blockers?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Because it is hydrophilic and penetrates the blood-brain barrier poorly, giving fewer CNS effects such as nightmares.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): how should dosing be adjusted in renal impairment?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It accumulates in renal impairment (renally cleared), so reduce the dose in CKD.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): which drugs must never be co-prescribed and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Never with verapamil or diltiazem -> additive AV block -> bradycardia, heart block, or asystole.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): why should it not be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia, angina, and hypertension -> taper the dose.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): what is the interaction with insulin/sulfonylureas?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It may mask the hypoglycaemia warning signs (except sweating).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): what should be monitored, and what resting HR target applies?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Monitor HR and BP, aiming for a resting HR not persistently below 50-55.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (atenolol): how is it used in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Uptitrate slowly and watch for transient worsening or fluid retention.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): what is propranolol's receptor selectivity and lipid solubility?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Non-selective beta-blocker (blocks both β1 and β2). Highly lipid-soluble, so it crosses the blood-brain barrier (giving CNS effects) and is hepatically metabolised.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): why is it called the 'non-cardiac' beta-blocker, and what are its main uses?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Because its key uses are outside cardiac indications: thyrotoxicosis, anxiety/somatic tremor, essential tremor, migraine prophylaxis, and portal hypertension (variceal bleed prophylaxis).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): how does it help in thyrotoxicosis?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It gives symptom control and blocks peripheral conversion of T4 -> T3.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): what are the main contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Asthma (non-selective block -> bronchospasm) and severe bradycardia / heart block.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): what is the typical regular oral dose?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 40 mg BD-TDS, up-titrated as needed.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): what is the dose for situational anxiety?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 10-40 mg PRN.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): what CNS side effects arise from its high lipid solubility?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Greater CNS penetration causes vivid dreams / nightmares and fatigue.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): which respiratory side effect makes it dangerous in asthma?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bronchospasm (from β2 blockade) - avoid in asthma.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): which drugs must never be combined with it, and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Never combine with verapamil or diltiazem -> additive AV block -> bradycardia, heart block, or asystole.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): why should it not be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia, angina, and hypertension - taper the dose instead.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): how does it interact with insulin/sulfonylureas?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It may mask the warning signs of hypoglycaemia (sweating is preserved).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): what should be monitored, and what resting HR target applies?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Monitor HR and BP; aim for a resting HR not persistently below 50-55.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers (propranolol): how should it be used in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Up-titrate slowly and watch for transient worsening / fluid retention.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: what is the mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, causing mild natriuresis. Long term they mainly lower BP by reducing peripheral vascular resistance.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: what are the indications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hypertension (NICE step 3 add-on) and mild oedema.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide-like diuretics: where do they sit in the NICE hypertension pathway, and which type is preferred?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Step 3 add-on. A thiazide-LIKE diuretic (e.g. indapamide) is preferred over a classic thiazide (e.g. bendroflumethiazide).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: what are the contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Gout/hyperuricaemia (urate rises, triggering attacks), hyponatraemia/hypokalaemia, Addison's disease, and severe renal or hepatic impairment.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: why is caution needed in diabetes?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They raise blood glucose.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: what is the typical dose of indapamide and bendroflumethiazide?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Indapamide 2.5 mg OD; bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg OD.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: what are the classic electrolyte side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia (classic - check U&Es), plus hypercalcaemia (Ca2+ retained).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: what metabolic side effects do they cause?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hyperuricaemia (precipitating gout), hyperglycaemia, and hyperlipidaemia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: name two non-metabolic side effects.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Postural hypotension and erectile dysfunction.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: what is the interaction with NSAIDs?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: NSAIDs blunt the diuretic/antihypertensive effect and increase the risk of AKI.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: what is the interaction with lithium?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They reduce lithium excretion, leading to lithium toxicity.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: what is the risk when combined with loop diuretics or steroids?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive hypokalaemia, which increases the risk of digoxin toxicity.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: what monitoring is required?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: U&Es (Na+, K+) at baseline and after starting or a dose change, as thiazides drop both. Also check glucose in diabetics and urate if gout-prone.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which drugs are thiazide-LIKE diuretics, and why are they NICE-preferred at step 3?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Indapamide and chlortalidone. They are longer-acting with better outcome data.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which drugs are classic thiazide diuretics, and what specific warning applies to hydrochlorothiazide?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bendroflumethiazide and hydrochlorothiazide. HCTZ carries an MHRA warning regarding non-melanoma skin cancer with long-term use.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: summarise the classic exam pearl on their metabolic effects.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They raise glucose, urate, calcium and lipids, and lower sodium and potassium - and can precipitate gout. Thiazide-like (indapamide) is preferred in hypertension.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what is the mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, producing powerful natriuresis/diuresis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what additional (non-renal) action gives rapid relief in pulmonary oedema?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They venodilate, which rapidly reduces preload and relieves pulmonary oedema.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what are the main clinical uses?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Fluid overload states: heart failure, pulmonary oedema, and nephrotic or hepatic oedema.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what is their place in hypertension treatment?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They are NOT a first-line antihypertensive; used when heart failure or CKD coexist.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what are the contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Severe hypokalaemia/hyponatraemia, dehydration/hypovolaemia, and anuria.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: in which conditions should they be used with caution?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Gout, hepatic encephalopathy, prostatic enlargement/urinary retention, and severe sulfonamide allergy (theoretical cross-reactivity, low in practice).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what is the typical furosemide dose?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Furosemide 40 mg OD PO (range 20-80 mg); given IV in acute pulmonary oedema.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: how does bumetanide dosing compare to furosemide?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bumetanide 1 mg is approximately equivalent to furosemide 40 mg, and is better absorbed when the gut is oedematous.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what electrolyte and acid-base disturbances do they cause?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia (lose Ca2+), and a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: how does their effect on calcium differ from thiazides?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Loops lose Ca2+ (hypocalcaemia), which is the opposite of thiazides, which retain calcium.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what non-electrolyte side effects can occur?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dehydration/AKI, hyperuricaemia (gout), ototoxicity (high-dose or fast IV), and hyperglycaemia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what interaction occurs with aminoglycosides?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive ototoxicity plus nephrotoxicity.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: why are they dangerous with digoxin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Loop-induced hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin toxicity.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what is the interaction with lithium?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They reduce lithium excretion, leading to lithium toxicity.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what should be monitored?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: U&Es (K+, Na+) and renal function, since loops drop K+ and can cause AKI if over-diuresed; use daily weights in acute heart failure to guide diuresis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: how does oral absorption differ between furosemide and bumetanide?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Furosemide has variable oral absorption that is worse when the gut is oedematous; bumetanide has better/more predictable oral absorption in gut oedema (1 mg ~ 40 mg furosemide).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: why must IV doses be given slowly?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: A fast IV bolus risks ototoxicity, so IV loops should be given slowly.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone): what is the mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block the mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) receptor in the distal nephron, producing mild natriuresis while retaining K+ (potassium-sparing).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: why are spironolactone and eplerenone used in heart failure with reduced EF?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They improve survival (prognostic benefit) and are added on top of an ACE inhibitor plus beta-blocker.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: what is their role in resistant hypertension per NICE?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Spironolactone is used at NICE step 4, but only if K+ is <=4.5.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: name other indications besides heart failure and resistant hypertension.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's), and ascites in cirrhosis (spironolactone is first-line for ascites).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: what are the contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hyperkalaemia (K+ >5.0), severe renal impairment, and Addison's disease.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: what is a key caution when combining with other drugs?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Combining with an ACE inhibitor or ARB requires close K+ monitoring due to additive hyperkalaemia risk.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Spironolactone: what is the typical dosing in heart failure and in ascites?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heart failure: 25 mg OD (range 12.5-50 mg). Ascites: up to 100-400 mg.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Eplerenone: what is the typical dose?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 25-50 mg OD.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: what is the key dangerous side effect?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hyperkalaemia, which can cause fatal arrhythmia; AKI is also a risk.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Spironolactone: what off-target sex-hormone side effects can it cause, and how does eplerenone differ?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Gynaecomastia, breast tenderness and menstrual upset (spironolactone is non-selective). Eplerenone is selective, so causes far less.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: which drugs cause additive hyperkalaemia when combined?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, K+ supplements, trimethoprim, and NSAIDs -> monitor K+ closely.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Spironolactone: what is its interaction with digoxin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Spironolactone can raise digoxin levels.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: how should U&Es be monitored?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check U&Es (K+, creatinine) before starting, at ~1 week and ~1 month, then periodically, to catch hyperkalaemia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: when should the drug be stopped based on monitoring?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Stop if K+ >6.0 or if AKI develops.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Aldosterone antagonists: if breast effects (gynaecomastia) occur on spironolactone, what is the recommended action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Switch to eplerenone, which is selective and does not cause gynaecomastia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Spironolactone: why does it have a slow onset (days) of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It acts largely via its long-lived active metabolite canrenone (t1/2 ~16 h); eplerenone is directly active with a shorter, cleaner profile.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene): what is their mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting duct, producing a mild natriuresis while sparing K+. This action is independent of aldosterone.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: what type of agent are amiloride and triamterene specifically (vs spironolactone-type drugs)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They are direct ENaC blockers, not aldosterone antagonists. They are weak diuretics used mainly to offset thiazide/loop-induced hypokalaemia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene): what is their main clinical use?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: As a potassium-sparing add-on, usually combined with a thiazide or loop diuretic to offset K+ loss (e.g. co-amilofruse). On their own they are only weak diuretics.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: what does the combination co-amilofruse contain and why is it used?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It combines amiloride (a K+-sparing ENaC blocker) with furosemide (a loop diuretic), pairing them so the amiloride offsets the loop-induced K+ loss.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene): what are the contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hyperkalaemia and severe renal impairment.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: in what situation should you use caution?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Caution when combined with an ACE inhibitor/ARB or other K+-sparing agents, because of the additive hyperkalaemia risk.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: what is the typical dose of amiloride?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Amiloride 5-10 mg once daily (OD).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene): what are the key side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hyperkalaemia and mild GI upset. Triamterene can rarely cause renal stones or AKI.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: which drug can rarely cause renal stones or AKI?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Triamterene.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: which drugs interact to cause additive hyperkalaemia?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, other K+-sparing agents, K+ supplements, trimethoprim, ciclosporin, and NSAIDs. These are additive, so check K+.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: how should amiloride/triamterene be monitored?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check U&E / K+ at baseline and after starting or any dose change (more often in renal impairment or with interacting drugs). Stop if the patient becomes hyperkalaemic.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics: what is the high-yield exam pearl?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They are weak diuretics used mainly to spare K+ alongside a thiazide/loop diuretic. Watch for hyperkalaemia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is the mechanism of action on blood pressure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block alpha-1 adrenoceptors on vascular smooth muscle -> vasodilation -> lower BP.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is their mechanism on the urinary tract?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They relax prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle -> improved urinary flow.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is their place in NICE hypertension management?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Resistant hypertension -> step 4 if K+ >4.5 (doxazosin).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: which drug is used for benign prostatic hyperplasia and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Tamsulosin -> it is uroselective (alpha-1A), so it treats BPH with minimal BP effect.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: in which patient groups should they be used with caution?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Caution with postural hypotension, the elderly (falls risk), and existing urinary incontinence.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is the starting dose and titration of doxazosin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Doxazosin 1 mg once daily, titrate up; modified-release up to 8 mg.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is the classic first-dose adverse effect and how do you prevent it?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: First-dose/postural hypotension and syncope -> give the first dose at bedtime (dose at night).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: list the common side effects besides postural hypotension.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dizziness, headache, ankle oedema, and urinary incontinence (in women).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what serious surgical complication is linked to tamsulosin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Intra-operative floppy iris syndrome -> warn the ophthalmologist before cataract surgery.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is the interaction with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive hypotension -> separate dosing/start low.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what happens if combined with other antihypertensives?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive hypotension -> separate dosing and start low.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is a key prescribing rule regarding combining these drugs?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Do not co-prescribe two alpha-blockers.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what monitoring is required?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Postural (lying/standing) BP, especially after the first dose and each uptitration.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what are the indications for doxazosin specifically?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: HTN (step 4) and BPH; the modified-release form smooths the postural BP drop.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is distinctive about tamsulosin's selectivity?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Uroselective (alpha-1A) -> used for BPH with minimal BP effect.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what are the indications for terazosin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Both HTN and BPH.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what is its mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Centrally-acting alpha2-agonist, acting via its metabolite alpha-methylnoradrenaline -> reduces central sympathetic outflow -> lowers BP.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what is its main clinical use?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hypertension in pregnancy. It is a recognised option with a long safety record, used where other agents are unsuitable.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): where does it sit in the treatment order for hypertension in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Not first-line. Labetalol is first-line, modified-release nifedipine is the usual alternative, and methyldopa is used where these are unsuitable.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what are its contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Depression (can precipitate or worsen it), active liver disease, and phaeochromocytoma.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what is the typical dosing?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 250 mg BD-TDS, up to a maximum of 3 g/day.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what are the common CNS/general side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Sedation/drowsiness, depression, dry mouth, and postural hypotension.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what haematological side effect can occur?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia (positive direct antiglobulin test).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what serious hepatic side effect can occur and how do you act on it?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Drug-induced hepatitis -> check LFTs.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): why are MAOIs contraindicated with it?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Risk of hypertensive crisis; the combination is contraindicated.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): how does it interact with oral iron salts?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Oral iron salts reduce methyldopa absorption -> separate the doses.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what is the interaction with lithium?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Enhanced lithium neurotoxicity.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what happens when combined with other antihypertensives or anaesthetics?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive hypotension.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what monitoring is required and when?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: LFTs (risk of drug-induced hepatitis) and FBC plus direct antiglobulin/Coombs test (haemolytic anaemia), at baseline and periodically.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what is the high-yield exam identity for this drug?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is the classic hypertension-in-pregnancy drug; watch for depression, sedation, and a positive Coombs test/haemolysis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Methyldopa (centrally acting): what should be done with it postnatally and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Stop it postnatally, because it worsens postnatal depression.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting antihypertensive): what is its mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is a centrally-acting imidazoline (I1) receptor agonist -> reduces central sympathetic outflow -> lowers BP.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Centrally-acting antihypertensives (moxonidine): what is the main indication?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Resistant hypertension -> a later-line option used when standard agents are unsuitable or insufficient.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): what are the cardiac contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Sick sinus syndrome, 2nd-3rd degree AV block, bradycardia <50 bpm, and severe heart failure.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): which allergy/reaction history is a contraindication?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: A history of angioedema.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): in which situations should it be used with caution?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Renal impairment and first-degree AV block.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): what is the typical dose?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 200 micrograms once daily, up to a maximum of 600 micrograms/day.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): what are the common side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dry mouth, headache, fatigue, and dizziness.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): why must it not be stopped abruptly, and what should you do instead?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension -> taper the dose rather than stopping suddenly.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): what interactions occur with other antihypertensives and CNS depressants?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive hypotension and sedation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): how do tricyclic antidepressants affect it?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Tricyclic antidepressants may reduce its antihypertensive effect.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): what should be monitored?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heart rate (HR) and blood pressure (BP).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): if a patient is also on a beta-blocker, in what order should the drugs be stopped?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Stop the moxonidine first (then the beta-blocker), tapering to avoid rebound hypertension.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Moxonidine (centrally-acting): what is the key high-yield exam pearl?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is a centrally-acting later-line add-on antihypertensive; do not stop abruptly as this causes rebound hypertension.
